claims.text: An integrated AIMD, rapid calorimetry, and CALPHAD approach can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across single-phase homogeneous HEAs.
Suitable starting materials are equiatomic, single-phase BCC or FCC HEAs produced to minimize segregation and inhomogeneity.
The proposed protocol combines rapid contactless calorimetry with high-throughput AIMD and CALPHAD modeling.
Using an inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during melting measurements.
Rapid heating with simultaneous pyrometric and calorimetric detection is suitable for measuring HEA melting behavior.
Chemical and microstructural homogeneity minimizes extrinsic effects from segregation and secondary phases.
Segregation and secondary phases can obscure intrinsic melting behavior.
AIMD can capture atomic-scale vibrational and configurational contributions near the melting transition.
Levitation calorimetry can precisely measure energy changes and volume expansion while avoiding container-interface effects.
CALPHAD can cross-validate the experimental and AIMD results and enable systematic extrapolation across HEA compositions.
The integrated approach will improve fusion-property accuracy by approximately 30–50% relative to traditional DSC.
The integrated approach is expected to achieve approximately 5–10% relative error.
Traditional DSC on bulk HEAs typically has approximately 10% error.
DSC inaccuracies arise from limited sample homogeneity and slow heating rates.
The approach is most applicable to HEAs that form single-phase solid solutions.
Multiphase HEAs can contain FCC and B2 phases.
The approach will be less reliable for multiphase, strongly segregated, or compositionally inhomogeneous HEAs because additional transformations can occur during melting.
Accurately capturing high-temperature vibrational entropy and liquid disorder in complex multicomponent systems may limit convergence between simulation and experiment.
Systematic deviations greater than approximately 10% across multiple alloys, or failure to reconcile simulation and experiment within stated uncertainty, would falsify the methodology.

contradictions.description: A 30–50% reduction from the stated DSC error of approximately 10% implies roughly 5–7% error, whereas the proposed uncertainty range extends to 10%, at which point there is no accuracy improvement over the stated baseline.
